strengths: Soundness: The main conditional Wasserstein bound has a coherent mathematical foundation. Theorem 4.1 combines reverse-ODE stability, log-Sobolev regularization under the OU process, and convergence of inexact Langevin dynamics. Appendices A–C provide detailed, checkable supporting arguments.

Significance: Keeping the forward horizon T1 independent of the desired sampling accuracy is a useful theoretical advance. The result covers norm-subgaussian targets without requiring the original data distribution to satisfy a log-Sobolev inequality, accommodating bounded and potentially singular distributions through early stopping.

Originality: Theorem 4.2 provides a substantive technical contribution: an explicit clipping operation uses proximity to the Gaussian score to convert terminal L2 estimation error into the exponential-moment control needed by the Langevin analysis. This adds new understanding to an algorithm assembled from established components.

Presentation, limitations, and ethics: The error decomposition and explanations of T1, T2, and early stopping make the analysis accessible. Section 6 appropriately acknowledges that a complete discretization theorem remains open. The theoretical and synthetic-data scope presents no apparent material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: The claim that ordinary integrated L2 score loss suffices needs qualification. Equations (4.3)–(4.4) retain the estimator-dependent factor I_tau(t), which depends exponentially on integrated one-sided Lipschitz constants. The convergence discussion on page 7 introduces an additional uniform regularity condition whose justification is heuristic; small L2 error does not imply such control. Theorem 4.2 also requires terminal error b(T1), which is not controlled by the integrated loss alone without further quantitative regularity.

The logarithmic dimension-dependence claim is too broad. The prescribed horizon T1 has logarithmic dependence, but the complete error bound includes sqrt(tau*d) and uncontrolled stability factors, while Proposition 6.1 contains explicit dimension and Lipschitz dependence. The manuscript does not establish logarithmic dependence for overall sampling accuracy or computational cost.

Practical complexity improvements remain unestablished. Proposition 6.1 gives an O(epsilon^-2 log(1/epsilon)) step bound for the Langevin initialization only. Reverse-ODE discretization, propagation of initialization error, and regularity as early stopping approaches zero are not included. Although Section 6 acknowledges this boundary, comparison with complete DDPM sampling bounds cannot establish an end-to-end speed advantage.

Empirical reproducibility is inadequate. Figure 1 omits the chosen T1 values, dataset-generation parameters, score-model architecture and training settings, numerical solvers, sample counts, Wasserstein estimation procedure, and meaning of the error bars. Its three toy examples also lack comparisons at matched computational budgets. Decreasing empirical Wasserstein distance does not establish that the exponential-moment error is small or that clipping is unnecessary.

There is a repairable normalization error in the preliminaries. For M=1, Equation (3.3) uses g times the score, whereas the probability-flow equation implied by (3.1)–(3.2) requires g^2/2 times the score; Equation (3.5) inherits this inconsistency. The OU-specific Equation (4.2) is correctly normalized, so this appears local rather than a failure of the main analysis.
